'''Jack St. Clair Kilby''' (November 8, 1923 – June 20, 2005) was an American [[electrical engineer]] who took part, along with [[Robert Noyce]] of [[Fairchild Semiconductor]], in the realization of the first [[integrated circuit]] while working at [[Texas Instruments]] in 1958.<ref name=":0" >{{Cite book |title=Electronic materials and processes handbook |date=2004 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |isbn=9780071402149 |editor-last=Harper |editor-first=Charles A. |edition=3 |series=McGraw-Hill handbooks }}</ref>{{Rp|page=22}} For this invention, Kilby shared the 2000 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]].<ref name="Nobel Prize">{{Cite web|title=Nobel Prize in Physics 2000 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/summary/|url-status=live |publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081021034902/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2000/index.html|archive-date=2008-10-21|access-date=2008-10-09}}</ref>

Kilby was also a co-inventor of the [[calculator|handheld calculator]] and the [[thermal printing|thermal printer]], for which he had the patents. He also had patents for seven other inventions.<ref name="IT Invention">{{cite web|title=The Chip that Jack Built|url=http://www.ti.com/corp/docs/kilbyctr/jackbuilt.shtml|publisher=IT Invention|access-date=May 27, 2014}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Jack St. Clair Kilby was born on November 8, 1923, in [[Jefferson City, Missouri]].<ref name="Britannica">{{Cite encyclopedia|title=Jack Kilby|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jack-Kilby|url-status=live |encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260407175058/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jack-Kilby |archive-date=2026-04-07|access-date=2026-04-01}}</ref> He was raised in [[Great Bend, Kansas]], where his father ran a small electric company that served customers in rural western Kansas. While in high school, a huge ice storm knocked down most of the poles that carried the telephone and electric power lines. His father's company had to use [[amateur radio]] operators for communication in the areas where customers had lost their power and phone service. This event sparked his interest in [[electronics]].<ref name="Nobel bio">{{Cite web|title=Jack Kilby – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/kilby/biographical/|url-status=live |publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20260427051858/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/kilby/biographical/|archive-date=2026-04-27|access-date=2026-06-28}}</ref>

After serving in the [[United States Army]] as an electronics technician during [[World War II]], Kilby entered the [[University of Illinois]], graduating in 1947 with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in Electrical Engineering.<ref name="Britannica"/><ref name="Grainger">{{Cite web|title=Jack S. Kilby |url=https://grainger.illinois.edu/alumni/hall-of-fame/jack-kilby|department=Grainger College of Engineering|publisher=University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|access-date=February 15, 2026}}</ref> He then joined the Centralab Division of Globe Union Inc. in [[Milwaukee, Wisconsin]], where he developed ceramic-base, silk-screen circuits for consumer electronic products.<ref name="Franklin">{{Cite web|title=Jack S. Kilby|url=https://fi.edu/en/awards/laureates/jack-s-kilby|url-status=live|publisher=Franklin Institute|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20250329195727/https://fi.edu/en/awards/laureates/jack-s-kilby |archive-date=2025-03-29|access-date=2026-02-15}}</ref> While working in Milwaukee, Kilby took evening classes at the [[University of Wisconsin]], where he received a [[Master of Science]] in Electrical Engineering in 1950.<ref name="Nobel bio"/><ref name="Kyoto Prize">{{Cite web|title=Jack St. Clair Kilby |url=https://www.kyotoprize.org/en/laureates/jack_st_clair_kilby/|url-status=live|publisher=Kyoto Prize|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20250205115021/https://www.kyotoprize.org/en/laureates/jack_st_clair_kilby/|archive-date=2025-02-05|access-date=2016-10-15}}</ref>

In 1952, Kilby visited [[Bell Telephone Laboratories]] to learn about the [[transistor]], which was invented there in 1947. After returning to Centralab, he began working on [[germanium]]-based transistors for use in [[hearing aid]]s. Due to needing the resources of a larger company to achieve [[miniaturization]] of circuits, he joined [[Texas Instruments]] (TI) in [[Dallas, Texas]], in 1958.<ref name="Britannica"/>

In 1970, Kilby took a leave of absence from TI to work as an independent inventor. He explored, among other subjects, the use of silicon technology for generating electrical power from sunlight. From 1978 to 1984, he was Distinguished Professor of Electrical Engineering at [[Texas A&M University]]. Although he officially retired from TI in the 1980s, Kilby remained involved with the company until his death in 2005.<ref name="Nobel bio"/>

== Invention of the integrated circuit ==
{{Main|Invention of the integrated circuit}}

[[Image:Kilby solid circuit.jpg|thumb|right|Kilby's original integrated circuit, 1958.]]

Kilby was vital to the invention of the [[integrated circuit]]. In mid-1958, as a newly employed engineer at [[Texas Instruments]] (TI), he did not yet have the right to a summer vacation. Kilby spent the summer working on the problem in circuit design that was commonly called the "[[tyranny of numbers]]," and he finally came to the conclusion that the manufacturing of circuit components ''en masse'' in a single piece of [[semiconductor]] material could provide a solution. On September 12, he presented his findings to company's management, which included [[Mark Shepherd (businessman)|Mark Shepherd]]. He showed them a piece of [[germanium]] with an [[oscilloscope]] attached, pressed a switch, and the oscilloscope showed a continuous [[sine wave]], proving that his integrated circuit worked, and thus that he had solved the problem.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Das|first=Saswato R.|date=September 19, 2008|title=Opinion: The chip that changed the world |language=en-US| work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/09/19/opinion/19iht-eddas.1.16308269.html }}</ref> U.S. Patent 3,138,743 for "Miniaturized electronic circuits," the first integrated circuit, was filed on February 6, 1959.<ref>{{Cite patent|status=patent|country=US|number=3138743|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US3138743A/en|invent1=Jack S Kilby|title=Miniaturized electronic circuits|gdate=1964-06-23|assign1=[[Texas Instruments Inc]]}}</ref> It was notable for having different components (transistors, diodes, resistors, capacitors, etc.) on one single substrate.{{r|:0|pp=22}} Along with [[Robert Noyce]] (who independently made a similar circuit a few months later), Kilby is generally credited as co-inventor of the integrated circuit.

== Other work ==
Kilby went on to pioneer military, industrial, and commercial applications of microchip technology. He headed teams that created the first military system and the first computer incorporating integrated circuits. He invented the handheld electronic [[calculator]] (along with [[Jerry Merryman]] and [[James Van Tassel]]<ref>{{cite news |last1=Stengle |first1=Jamie |title=Jerry Merryman, co-inventor of handheld electronic calculator, dies at 86 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/jerry-merryman-co-inventor-of-handheld-electronic-calculator-dies-at-86/2019/03/07/801f910c-413c-11e9-922c-64d6b7840b82_story.html |access-date=March 8, 2019 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=March 7, 2019}}</ref>), showing a prototype called "Cal Tech" in 1967, which lead to the commercial [[Canon Inc.|Canon]] "Pocketronic" in 1971.

== Family ==
In 1948, Kilby married Barbara Annegers. They had two daughters, Ann and Janet.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kilby, Jack S. (Jack St. Clair), 1923-2005|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11603012.html|url-status=dead|publisher=American Institute of Physics|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20250613001535/https://history.aip.org/phn/11603012.html|archive-date=2025-06-13|access-date=2026-02-15}}</ref>

== Death and legacy ==
Kilby died of cancer on June 20, 2005, in [[Dallas, Texas]], at the age of 81.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/06/22/business/jack-s-kilby-an-inventor-of-the-microchip-is-dead-at-81.html|title=Jack S. Kilby, an Inventor of the Microchip, Is Dead at 81 |date=June 22, 2005|author=John Markoff| work=New York Times|access-date=January 9, 2022}}</ref>

On December 14, 2005, [[Texas Instruments]] created the Historic TI Archives. The Jack Kilby family donated his personal manuscripts and his personal photograph collection to [[Southern Methodist University|Southern Methodist University (SMU)]]. The collection will be cataloged and stored at DeGolyer Library, SMU.

In 2008, the SMU School of Engineering, with the DeGolyer Library and the Library of Congress, hosted a year-long celebration of the 50th anniversary of the birth of the digital age with Kilby's Nobel Prize-winning invention of the integrated circuit. Symposia and exhibits examined the many ways in which technology and engineers shaped the modern world. Kilby held an honorary doctorate of science from SMU and was a longtime associate of SMU through the Kilby Foundation.

== Commemoration ==
The Kilby Award Foundation was founded in 1980 in his honor, and the [[IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal]] was created in 1995.

The Kilby Labs, TI's research laboratory for [[silicon]] manufacturing and [[integrated circuit]] design, is named after him.

The Jack Kilby Computer Centre at the [[Merchiston]] Campus of [[Edinburgh Napier University]] in [[Edinburgh]] is also named in his honor.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.napier.ac.uk/soc/studying/Pages/facilities.aspx |title=School of Computing – Facilities & Resources |publisher=Edinburgh Napier University |access-date={{Format date|2012|7|24}} |archive-date=June 25, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130625145615/http://www.napier.ac.uk/soc/studying/Pages/facilities.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref>

A statue of Jack Kilby stands in Texas Instruments Plaza on the campus of The University of Texas at Dallas.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What’s the Story? The TI Plaza Statue |url=https://magazine.utdallas.edu/2022/06/08/whats-the-story-the-ti-plaza-statue/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=UT Dallas Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

Barton Community College in Great Bend, Kansas, holds an annual Jack Kilby STEM Day.<ref>{{Cite web |title=21st Annual Jack Kilby STEM Day |url=https://bartonccc.edu/jack-kilby-stem-day |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Barton Community College}}</ref>
